then we will return into open for the delegation.
I think that we're good to go to close, everybody

Okay, colleagues, can I have a mover in a second
or a motion to reconvene? Councillor James, Councillor Erb. All
those in favor? Just show a hands would be great.
That is passed. We'll now call upon our delegation. Sam.
Nabi, you've got five minutes. Good morning.
Thank you, Chair Harris, members of council, for the opportunity
to speak. My name is Sam Nabi. I'm a hip
hop artist and arts organizer in the region. I was
a festival organizer for Hold the Line Cycling and Folk
Music Festival. Mel Brown Music Festival Gaukel Street Pop up
Park, and I was also part of the Arts Fund,
Imagine Equitable Futures consultation that I participated in during 2021
and 2022. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. About
the arts fund and some of the recent decisions that
have occurred with relation to arts funding in the region.
In 2022, there were two reports prepared for the previous
arts fund board. They contained a number of recommendations, many
of which were initiated by the previous board, and this
includes creating different funding streams for emerging and established artists,
creating paid peer review positions and prioritizing black, Indigenous and
people of color artists to be over 50% of the
successful guarantees. That was some of the policies that were
enacted and were in progress. There were clearly some major
issues with the way the spring 2023 round of funding
was managed. With only 6% of successful grantees in those
priority categories. Artists in my community were disappointed that the
good equity work that had been happening didn't seem to
be bearing out in practice. We hope the fund would
tweak its processes, add some more checks and balances to
the peer review process and deliver a more equitable round
of funding in fall 2023. Unfortunately, the new board made
the decision to not have a fall round of funding
at all. That's when uncertainty turned to disbelief for a
lot of artists that I know. The purpose of an
arts fund is to fund art, and it hasn't been
fulfilling its core mandate for the past seven or eight
months. So given these circumstances, I do think the decision
to have the Waterloo Region Community Foundation administer this year's funding
was the right one. At a recent town hall meeting
for the save the arts campaign, the chair of the
Arts Fund revealed that there was about $100,000 left from
the money that has been earmarked for fall 2023. It
was unclear what the rest of the money for that
round has been spent on. There were two equity reports
that had already been completed in 2022. But regardless, the
remaining money was intended to carry forward into 2024, and
I hope that it has been added to the total
pot of money being distributed by the Community Foundation this
year. I believe the Community Foundation will do a good
job administering this year's grants. I've sat on granting committees
with them before, they have processes in place to allocate
funds, based on a number of priorities, including geographic representation,
Indigenous representation, gender diversity. I hope they're able to integrate
some of these recommendations from the imagining equitable futures work
that has been done over the past couple of years
at the Arts Fund and I also hope that we
come out the other side with a strengthened Region of
Waterloo Arts Fund that has the administrative support it needs
to do the work of funding artists. While art and
community often overlap, I wouldn't want to see everything lumped
into one organization. The Arts fund, is worth keeping as
an arm's length, municipally funded body and I know many
of my colleagues in the art scene are eager to
see it return to form in 2025. I can see
a future where it could expand to include funding for
key cultural institutions and remove some of the political decisions
around funding individual organizations that have been undertaken by this
committee. There was also a comment made in last month's
committee meeting about trying to understand if some of the
projects, funded through the region's equity focused funds, are also
helping the arts. I think this is the wrong way
to look at it. If a project with an art
component for example, is funded through upstream, that shouldn't take
away the importance of funding art through its own dedicated
program. Art is important for its own sake, not only
when it is paired with another cause and we shouldn't
look to other equity focused grants to downplay the responsibility
of the arts fund to implement those equity recommendations. Thank
you for your time. I look forward to learning more
about the third party review of the arts fund, and
I hope it will return stronger than ever as a
core part of the region's support for the arts. Thank
you. Thank you, Sam. Colleagues Chair Redman. Sam, thank you
very much for coming in. I'm just wondering, as we
go forward and we do some consultations as to what
the next iteration might look like. Would you be willing
to participate? I know you have in the past. Yes,
absolutely. Thank you. I don't see any other questions. Sam,
thank you for your time this morning and your patience
with us. Colleagues. We have no reports this month, but
we do have the tracking list to receive for information.
Is there any other business? Any other new business. Seeing
none. We will, I guess, look forward to our next
meeting, which I hear is more of a robust agenda
on April the 9th, 2024. I'd ask now for consideration
of a motion to go into closed, do I
have a mover? Councillor Wolf. Seconded by Councillor James. All
those in favor? Carried and will now also ask for
a motion to adjourn. Motion moved by Councillor Wolf, Councillor
Salonen all those in favor carried. We will resume the
closed session in the Waterloo County room and then return for our final committee of the day.
